lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand the problems arising from pollutants from the combustion of alkane fuels, limited to the toxicity of carbon monoxide and why it is toxic, and the acidity of oxides of nitrogen and sulfur

primer.text: Every flame writes a pollution ledger. Carbon monoxide silently occupies the haemoglobin sites meant for oxygen; sulfur and nitrogen oxides from engines and impure fuels return as acid rain. This note names each pollutant, its origin, its damage and the removal chemistry that limits it, table by table.

modules.title: Carbon monoxide: the silent poison
modules.opening: Exhaust fumes concentrate the combustion problems of alkane fuels into one pipe. The deadliest passenger is carbon monoxide, born of incomplete combustion, whose toxicity comes from a molecular hijack: it occupies the haemoglobin sites that oxygen needs.
keyPoints: Car exhaust fumes carry toxic gases, chiefly carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion.
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.
Occupied haemoglobin sites cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's delivery capacity collapses.
The gas is colourless and odourless, so exposure gives no sensory warning.
Adequate oxygen supply at the flame prevents the carbon monoxide from forming in the first place.

low.restatement: CO forms when a flame runs short of oxygen; once inhaled it grabs the blood's oxygen seats so firmly that oxygen cannot board, and the victim suffocates without noticing.
low.analogy: CO is a passenger who boards the bus (haemoglobin) first and refuses to get off, leaving the real passengers (oxygen) stranded at the stop.
low.examPointer: Quote the haemoglobin mechanism explicitly - 'prevents oxygen transport' is the marking phrase, not merely 'it is toxic'.

medium.restatement: The affinity gap is the whole story: carbon monoxide occupies the iron centres of haemoglobin preferentially, and because the complex is stable, even low concentrations accumulate across the red-cell fleet until delivery fails.
medium.analogy: A stronger magnet (CO) keeps snapping onto every iron filing (haemoglobin site) before the weaker one (O2) can attach.
medium.examPointer: Tie the hazard to the combustion condition: the cure is complete combustion through adequate air supply and maintained appliances.

modules.title: Oxides of sulfur and nitrogen: acid rain chemistry
modules.opening: Two families of oxides carry the acidity problem. Sulfur dioxide rises from sulfur impurities burned in fuels; nitrogen oxides form inside engines where air's nitrogen and oxygen meet flame temperatures. Both return to earth as acid rain.
keyPoints: Sulfur dioxide forms when sulfur impurities in fossil fuels burn.
Oxides of nitrogen form when nitrogen and oxygen from air combine at engine temperatures.
Sulfur dioxide dissolves in atmospheric moisture to give acidic solutions that fall as acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides likewise contribute to acid rain and to photochemical pollution.
Neither oxide family comes from the alkane itself - sulfur is an impurity and nitrogen comes from the air.

low.restatement: Fuel impurities give sulfur dioxide; engine heat welds air's nitrogen and oxygen into nitrogen oxides; both dissolve in clouds and fall as acid rain.
low.analogy: Two factories, one chimney: the fuel brings the sulfur, the engine's heat manufactures the nitrogen oxides, and the sky delivers the combined bill as acid.
low.examPointer: Attribute the sources correctly: sulfur dioxide from impurities, nitrogen oxides from air at high temperature - swapping them is the classic error.

medium.restatement: The acidity pathway runs through dissolution and oxidation: sulfur dioxide becomes sulfurous then sulfuric acid in atmospheric water, while nitrogen oxides convert to nitric acid, so the rainfall pH drops wherever the emissions concentrate.
medium.analogy: Each oxide is a scheduled delivery of acid: the cloud is the warehouse and the rain is the delivery van.
medium.examPointer: Name both acid rain contributors when asked for pollutants from combustion - the specification pairs sulfur and nitrogen oxides.

modules.title: The pollutant ledger and its removal chemistry
modules.opening: Reading the pollutant table is a matching exercise with consequences: each gas carries an effect and pairs with a removal technology. Catalytic converters handle the nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide pair; flue-gas scrubbing handles sulfur dioxide.
keyPoints: The pollutant table pairs each gas with its effect and its removal method.
Catalytic converters reduce nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide at the exhaust together.
Flue-gas desulfurisation removes sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions using basic absorbents.
Calcium carbonate scrubbing converts sulfur dioxide into a solid sulfite waste.
Matching the right removal method to the right pollutant is the exam's core demand.

low.restatement: One table, three rows: carbon monoxide poisons blood and meets catalytic converters; nitrogen oxides acidify rain and meet converters too; sulfur dioxide acidifies rain and meets calcium carbonate scrubbing.
low.analogy: Each pollutant has its own dentist: converters clean the exhaust pair, scrubbers clean the power-station gas.
low.examPointer: Never attach scrubbing to the exhaust or converters to power-station flue gases - the methods are site-specific.

medium.restatement: The removal chemistry is acid-base at heart: acidic oxides (SO2, NOx-derived acids) meet basic absorbers, while the converter runs redox rearrangements that turn CO and NO into CO2 and N2.
medium.analogy: Scrubbing is an antacid tablet for the flue; the converter is a recycling plant re-sorting two poisons into two harmless products.
medium.examPointer: Write the converter equation 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2 when asked how converters limit pollution - it earns the mechanism mark.

glossary.definition: The toxic product of incomplete combustion that occupies haemoglobin sites and blocks oxygen transport.
Rainfall acidified by dissolved sulfur and nitrogen oxides from combustion emissions.
The exhaust device converting carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
Scrubbing sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions with a basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate.
